0:58 intentionally misleading graph is crappy. Between 1,000 and 3,000? Why is it zoomed out so much with data points so much higher than 3k to go up over 10k then? The reason, obviously, is to mislead viewers. Because 3x-ing in 30 years isn’t that bad. And it isn’t THAT flat. But if you add 10,000 plus on the y axis, of course the line is going to look flat. And that’s what you want to portray so you were fine showing such a misleading graph as it better exemplifies the point you’re saying.  This was the worst way to start the video and loses a lot of credibility with me. You didn’t need to do that. You could have put it as one color line on an overlaid graph showing several different markets to show how flat it is in comparison, and then it would also make sense to have those high data points on the y, and it wouldn’t be misleading at all while much better proving your point. But if you only use one line, then you have to crunch the graph to better points on the y. 5th grade lessons on making graphs told us that this isn’t how you do it. A teacher would dock points on a child’s presentation for making a graph like this. It’s actually ridiculous, and you need to be called out for it.

Edit: after watching the rest of the video, I have a feeling that you zoomed in on the graph, and the reason it goes up to 10k is because on the missing right side of the graph is where the KOSPI just went up to 8,000+. Fair. But would’ve been way better to show that when showing the graph, as it would’ve also really made obvious why the first part going from 1000-3000 was called “flat,” because of just how fast it rose recently. That would’ve been justifiable. Still maintain my complaint, but I see that your desire I guess to not spoil the video and get to reveal incrementally just how high the market went before crashing pushed you not to show the whole graph early on… anyway. Still dislike showing such a misleading graph, but I have a feeling the graph itself was actually less misleading and more just missing half of it on screen.
